name: Apple

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Skin should be vibrant and free of bruises or wrinkles. A slight sheen indicates freshness.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel firm and heavy for its size. Soft spots mean it is past its peak.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A sweet, fruity aroma near the stem end indicates ripeness. No smell often means it was picked too early.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: The stem should be intact. A missing stem lets air in and speeds spoilage.

funFact: There are over 7,500 apple varieties grown worldwide, though most grocery stores carry only about 5 to 10.
storageTip: Store in the crisper drawer of the refrigerator for up to 6 weeks. Keep away from other produce, as apples release ethylene gas that speeds ripening.

name: Apricot

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be uniformly golden-orange with no green patches. A slight blush of red is fine.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Gently press the fruit: it should give slightly but not feel mushy. Too firm means it is underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Ripe apricots have a sweet, floral fragrance. If there is no scent, they are not ready.

funFact: Apricots were cultivated in China over 4,000 years ago before traveling along the Silk Road to the Mediterranean.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature stem-side down, then refrigerate for up to 5 days. Do not wash until ready to eat.

name: Avocado

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Gently squeeze without pressing fingertips in. It should yield to gentle pressure when ripe.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Hass avocados turn dark purplish-black when ripe. Green varieties stay green, so rely on feel.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: Flick off the small stem cap. If it comes off easily and is green underneath, it is ripe. Brown underneath means overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A ripe avocado should feel heavy for its size, indicating it still has moisture.

funFact: Avocados do not ripen on the tree; farmers can leave them hanging for months as a form of natural storage.
storageTip: Ripen on the counter in 2 to 5 days. To speed it up, place in a paper bag with a banana. Once ripe, refrigerate for up to 3 days.

name: Banana

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Yellow with small brown freckles is the sweet spot. Fully green means underripe; mostly brown means best for baking.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm but not hard. The peel should give slightly under gentle pressure.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A ripe banana has a sweet, pleasant fragrance at the stem end.

funFact: Bananas are technically berries, while strawberries are not; botanists classify them based on seed and flower structure.
storageTip: Store at room temperature until ripe. To slow ripening, wrap the stem in plastic wrap. Refrigerating turns the peel brown but the fruit inside stays good for several days.

name: Blueberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deep indigo-blue with a silvery-white bloom (natural waxy coating). Red or green tinges mean underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be plump and firm. Squeeze the container gently; berries should move freely, not stick together in clumps.

ripenessTips.title: Check container
ripenessTips.description: Flip the container and look for juice stains or crushed berries at the bottom, which indicate damage.

funFact: Blueberries are one of the only natural foods that are truly blue; the color comes from anthocyanin pigments.
storageTip: Do not wash until ready to eat. Store in the refrigerator in a single layer on a paper towel for up to 10 days. Freeze on a sheet pan before transferring to a bag.

name: Cantaloupe

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The rind under the netting should be golden or cream-colored, not green. The blossom end should have a slight give.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sniff the stem end. A ripe cantaloupe has a sweet, musky aroma. No scent means it is underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy for its size. The stem end should be slightly indented, meaning it slipped off the vine when ripe.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Tap the outside. A deep, low sound indicates the flesh is dense and juicy.

funFact: What Americans call cantaloupe is actually a muskmelon; true cantaloupes have a smoother rind and are more common in Europe.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature until fragrant, then refrigerate and eat within 3 to 5 days. Cut melon should be wrapped and eaten within 2 days.

name: Cherry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deeply colored: dark red to almost black for sweet varieties, bright red for sour. Avoid pale or shriveled cherries.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be plump and firm with glossy, taut skin. Soft or wrinkled cherries are past their prime.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: Green, flexible stems indicate freshness. Brown, brittle stems mean they have been sitting too long.

funFact: Cherry trees are related to roses, almonds, and peaches, all belonging to the Prunus genus in the Rosaceae family.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a single layer in the refrigerator for up to a week. Bring to room temperature before eating for best flavor. Freeze pitted cherries on a sheet pan.

name: Cranberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deep red with a glossy, smooth surface. Pale or white berries are underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: A ripe cranberry is firm and bounces when dropped on a hard surface. Soft berries should be discarded.

ripenessTips.title: Inspect
ripenessTips.description: Check the bag for moisture or crushed berries. Dry, firm berries in a clean bag will last the longest.

funFact: Cranberries have small air pockets inside, which is why they float in water and can be wet-harvested by flooding the bogs.
storageTip: Refrigerate in their original bag for up to 2 months. Freeze in a single layer, then bag them; frozen cranberries last up to a year.

name: Fig

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be plump and slightly drooping at the neck. Color depends on variety: deep purple, green, or brown.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: A ripe fig yields to gentle pressure like a ripe peach. Rock-hard figs were picked too early and will not ripen well.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Should smell sweet and jammy. A sour or fermented smell means it is overripe.

funFact: Figs are technically inverted flowers; the tiny seeds inside are the actual fruits of the plant.
storageTip: Figs are highly perishable. Store on a plate lined with paper towel in the refrigerator and eat within 2 to 3 days of purchase.

name: Grape

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be plump with consistent color. A whitish bloom on the surface is natural and indicates freshness.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Pick up the bunch and shake gently. A few grapes may fall, but many dropping indicates they are past peak.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: The stem should be green and flexible. A brown, dry, or brittle stem means old grapes.

funFact: A single grapevine can produce enough fruit to make about 10 bottles of wine, and some vines live for over 100 years.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a ventilated bag or container in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks. Wash just before eating.

name: Grapefruit

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Pick it up: a ripe grapefruit is surprisingly heavy for its size, indicating high juice content.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm but springy with smooth, thin skin. Thick, puffy skin often means less juice inside.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Color varies by variety but should be vibrant. Slight green tinge on otherwise colored fruit is fine.

funFact: Grapefruit got its name because it grows in clusters on the tree, similar to how grapes grow in bunches.
storageTip: Store at room temperature for about a week, or refrigerate for up to 6 weeks. Bring to room temperature before eating for the juiciest flavor.

name: Kiwi

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Press gently with your thumb. A ripe kiwi gives slightly, like a ripe pear. Rock-hard means it needs more time.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The fuzzy brown skin should be intact without wrinkles, dark spots, or mold.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A ripe kiwi has a light, fruity fragrance. A strong or fermented smell indicates it is overripe.

funFact: Kiwis were originally called Chinese gooseberries; New Zealand growers renamed them after their national bird for marketing appeal.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature away from sunlight. Once ripe, store in the refrigerator for up to 4 weeks. To speed ripening, place in a bag with a banana.

name: Lemon

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be bright, vibrant yellow with smooth, fine-grained skin. Pale or greenish lemons tend to be more acidic.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Choose lemons that are firm but give slightly. Thin-skinned lemons yield more juice than thick-skinned ones.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A juicy lemon feels heavy for its size. Lightweight lemons have dried out inside.

funFact: Lemon juice is a natural preservative; its citric acid prevents cut fruits like apples and avocados from browning.
storageTip: Store at room temperature for a week, or in a sealed bag in the refrigerator for up to a month. A whole lemon kept in water in the fridge stays juicy even longer.

name: Mango

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sniff the stem end. A ripe mango has a strong, sweet, fruity aroma. No smell means it needs more time.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should yield gently to pressure, like a ripe avocado. Very firm is underripe; mushy is overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Color depends on variety and is not the best indicator. Focus on feel and smell instead. Avoid any with wrinkled or oozing skin.

funFact: Mangoes are the most consumed fruit in the world, with over 400 varieties grown across tropical regions.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature until fragrant and slightly soft. Once ripe, refrigerate for up to 5 days. Cut mango can be frozen for smoothies.

name: Orange

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A heavy orange means more juice. Compare similarly sized oranges and pick the heaviest one.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm with smooth, thin skin. Puffy or spongy skin usually means less juice and more pith.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: A slight green tinge does not mean unripe; oranges sometimes regreen. Uniform shape is a better indicator of quality.

funFact: The color orange was actually named after the fruit, not the other way around; before that, English speakers called the color 'geoluhread' (yellow-red).
storageTip: Store at room temperature for about a week, or in the refrigerator for up to 3 weeks. Roll on the counter before juicing to get more juice out.

name: Peach

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A ripe peach has a strong, sweet fragrance you can smell from arm's length. No scent likely means no flavor.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should give slightly to gentle pressure, especially along the seam. Avoid rock-hard or mushy fruit.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The background color (not the blush) tells ripeness. It should be golden or creamy, not green.

funFact: Despite being called Persian apples in many languages, peaches originated in China where they have been cultivated for over 8,000 years.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature stem-side down. Once ripe, refrigerate for up to 5 days. Cold peaches lose some flavor, so bring back to room temperature before eating.

name: Pear

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Press gently near the stem. If it yields slightly, it is ripe. Pears ripen from the inside out, so the flesh is ready before the skin shows it.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Color change varies by type. Bartlett pears turn yellow; Bosc stay brown. Check the neck, not the body.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A sweet, floral fragrance near the stem means it is ready. If there is no aroma, it needs more time.

funFact: Pears are one of the few fruits that ripen better off the tree; left on the branch they develop a gritty texture from stone cells.
storageTip: Buy firm and ripen at room temperature for a few days. Once the neck yields to gentle pressure, refrigerate for up to 5 days.

name: Persimmon

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deep orange to reddish-orange with glossy skin. Green patches indicate immaturity.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Hachiya persimmons should be jelly-soft when ripe. Fuyu types can be eaten when still firm, like an apple.

ripenessTips.title: Check leaves
ripenessTips.description: The calyx (leaf cap) should be flat against the fruit and green. A dried, pulling-away calyx means it is old.

funFact: Unripe Hachiya persimmons contain high levels of tannins that cause an intense, mouth-puckering astringency that vanishes when fully ripe.
storageTip: Ripen Hachiyas at room temperature until very soft, which can take a week or more. Fuyu types store for a few weeks in the fridge. Freeze puree for baking.

name: Pineapple

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sniff the base. A strong, sweet, tropical aroma means it is ripe. No smell means bland fruit; fermented smell means overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be golden-yellow from the base up. More yellow means sweeter. Leaves should be green, not brown.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel firm but give slightly when pressed. A leaf from the center crown should pull out with gentle effort when ripe.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy for its size, meaning it is full of juice.

funFact: A pineapple is actually a cluster of 100 to 200 individual berries fused together around a central core.
storageTip: A pineapple will not ripen further after picking; it only gets softer. Store upside down at room temperature for 1 to 2 days to distribute sweetness. Refrigerate cut pineapple for up to 5 days.

name: Pomegranate

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Should feel surprisingly heavy; the weight comes from juice-filled arils inside.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Skin should be deep red and taut. Slight angularity of the sides (not perfectly round) means the arils are full.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: The skin should be firm and leathery, not soft or cracked. Small scratches on the surface do not affect quality.

funFact: A single pomegranate contains about 600 to 800 arils (seed pods), each wrapped in a jewel-like sac of juice.
storageTip: Whole pomegranates last up to 2 months in the refrigerator. Store arils in an airtight container in the fridge for up to a week, or freeze them for months.

name: Strawberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be uniformly bright red from tip to stem with no white or green patches. White shoulders mean underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: The most reliable test: ripe strawberries have a strong, sweet berry fragrance. No smell means no flavor.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm but not hard. Avoid soft, mushy, or leaking berries.

ripenessTips.title: Check cap
ripenessTips.description: The green cap should be bright and fresh-looking, firmly attached. Wilted caps mean they were picked days ago.

funFact: Strawberries are the only fruit that wears its seeds on the outside, with about 200 tiny seeds on each berry.
storageTip: Do not wash until ready to eat. Store in a single layer on paper towels in the refrigerator for 3 to 5 days. Moldy berries should be removed immediately as mold spreads fast.

name: Watermelon

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Check the field spot where it rested on the ground. A creamy yellow spot indicates ripeness; white means underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Knock on it. A ripe watermelon produces a deep, hollow sound. A dull thud means it may be overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Should feel very heavy for its size. Watermelons are 92 percent water, so weight means juiciness.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: The rind should be hard and resist scratching with a fingernail. A slightly bumpy surface texture is normal.

funFact: Watermelon is both a fruit and a vegetable; it belongs to the cucumber and squash family (Cucurbitaceae).
storageTip: Store whole at room temperature for up to 2 weeks. Cut watermelon should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within 5 days.

name: Artichoke

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should be tightly packed, firm, and green. Spreading or browning leaves mean it is past its prime.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy and dense for its size. Squeeze it: a fresh artichoke squeaks slightly.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Squeeze the artichoke near your ear. A fresh one makes a squeaking sound as the leaves press together.

funFact: The part of the artichoke we eat is actually an immature flower bud; if left unharvested, it blooms into a large, purple thistle.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. Sprinkle a few drops of water in the bag to keep them hydrated.

name: Asparagus

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Tips should be tightly closed and compact, not flowering or mushy. Stalks should be bright green or purple.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Stalks should be firm and straight, snapping cleanly when bent. Limp asparagus is old.

ripenessTips.title: Check base
ripenessTips.description: The cut ends should look fresh and moist, not dried out, woody, or excessively white.

funFact: Asparagus is one of the fastest growing vegetables, capable of growing up to 10 inches in a single day under ideal conditions.
storageTip: Treat like cut flowers: trim the ends and stand upright in a jar with an inch of water, covered loosely with a plastic bag. Refrigerate and use within 3 to 5 days.

name: Beetroot

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deep, rich color with smooth skin. Avoid beets with scales, bruises, or soft wet spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be very firm and hard, like a rock. Soft beets are old. Smaller beets tend to be sweeter and more tender.

ripenessTips.title: Check greens
ripenessTips.description: If greens are still attached, they should be vibrant and not wilted. Fresh greens indicate a freshly harvested beet.

funFact: Beets were originally cultivated for their greens only; eating the root did not become popular until the 1500s in Germany.
storageTip: Remove greens immediately as they draw moisture from the root. Store unwashed roots in a plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to 3 weeks. Cook greens separately within 2 days.

name: Bell Pepper

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should have vibrant, glossy skin with no wrinkles or dull patches. Color should be uniform throughout.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm with thick walls that do not flex easily when pressed. Avoid soft spots or thin walls.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A heavy pepper has thick, juicy walls. Lighter ones tend to have thinner flesh.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: The stem should be bright green and firmly attached. A brown or withered stem signals age.

funFact: Green bell peppers are actually unripe; if left on the plant they turn yellow, then orange, then red, getting sweeter at each stage.
storageTip: Store unwashed in the crisper drawer for up to 2 weeks. Cut peppers should be stored in an airtight container and used within 3 days.

name: Broccoli

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Florets should be tightly closed and dark green to blue-green. Yellowing florets mean it is starting to flower and past peak.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: The head should be firm and the stalk should feel crisp when snapped. Rubbery stalks indicate old broccoli.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Fresh broccoli has a mild, slightly green scent. A strong, cabbage-like odor means it is getting old.

funFact: Broccoli is a human invention, bred by Italian farmers from wild cabbage plants starting in the 6th century BCE.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a loose plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Do not seal tightly as broccoli needs some airflow. Do not wash before storing.

name: Brussels Sprouts

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be bright green with tightly packed leaves. Avoid any with black spots or yellowing outer leaves.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm and compact. Loose or puffy sprouts will be bitter and have a cabbage-like taste.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Smaller sprouts (about 1 inch) tend to be sweeter and more tender than larger ones.

funFact: Brussels sprouts taste less bitter after a frost because the cold triggers the plant to convert starches into sugars as a natural antifreeze.
storageTip: Store in a bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. If still on the stalk, they keep even longer. Trim and halve right before cooking.

name: Cabbage

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel very heavy and solid when picked up. The head should be compact with no give when squeezed.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Outer leaves should be vibrant and fresh, not wilted, yellowed, or slimy. Check the stem end for signs of browning.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Compare cabbages of similar size; the heavier one is denser and fresher.

funFact: Cabbage was one of the first vegetables cultivated by Europeans, and sauerkraut was reportedly fed to workers building the Great Wall of China.
storageTip: Whole, unwashed cabbage will keep in the crisper drawer for up to 2 months. Once cut, wrap tightly in plastic wrap and use within 5 days.

name: Carrot

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be bright orange with smooth skin. Cracks, green shoulders, or forking indicate poor growing conditions.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm and rigid, not bendy or limp. A bendable carrot has lost its moisture.

ripenessTips.title: Check greens
ripenessTips.description: If tops are attached, they should be bright green and feathery. Wilted tops mean the carrot is not fresh.

funFact: Carrots were originally purple and yellow; the orange variety was developed in the Netherlands in the 17th century.
storageTip: Remove greens immediately as they pull moisture from the root. Store in a sealed bag in the crisper drawer for up to 3 weeks. Limp carrots can be revived by soaking in ice water.

name: Cauliflower

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The head should be creamy white (or uniformly colored for purple/green varieties) with no brown or dark spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be heavy and firm with compact, tightly packed florets. Loose, spreading florets indicate over-maturity.

ripenessTips.title: Check leaves
ripenessTips.description: The surrounding leaves should be green and crisp, hugging the head. Wilted or yellow leaves mean it is old.

funFact: Cauliflower is available in purple, orange, and green varieties, each with slightly different nutritional profiles and flavors.
storageTip: Store whole, unwashed, stem-side up in a loosely closed bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. Cut florets last about 4 days.

name: Corn

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Through the husk, the ear should feel plump with kernels you can feel from top to bottom. Gaps mean poor pollination.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The silk at the top should be brown and slightly sticky, not dry and black. Green husks should be tightly wrapped.

ripenessTips.title: Check kernels
ripenessTips.description: Peel back a small section of husk. Kernels should be plump and release milky liquid when pierced. Clear liquid means underripe.

funFact: Corn always has an even number of rows on each ear, typically between 12 and 16, due to the way the kernels develop in pairs.
storageTip: Eat as soon as possible; corn starts converting sugar to starch within hours of picking. Store in the husk in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Do not shuck until ready to cook.

name: Cucumber

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be dark green and uniform with no yellowing, which indicates over-maturity and bitter seeds.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be very firm from end to end. Soft ends mean the cucumber is aging and the inside is getting mushy.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Medium-sized cucumbers have the best flavor and texture. Very large ones tend to be seedy and bitter.

funFact: Cucumbers are 96 percent water, making them one of the most hydrating foods available.
storageTip: Wrap individually in a paper towel and store in a loose bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. Keep away from tomatoes and bananas which speed deterioration.

name: Eggplant

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should have smooth, glossy, taut skin with consistent deep purple color. Dull or wrinkled skin means it is old.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Press gently with your thumb. It should spring back. If the indent stays, it is overripe. If rock-hard, it is underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy for its size. Lightweight eggplants can be spongy and bitter inside.

ripenessTips.title: Check cap
ripenessTips.description: The green calyx and stem should look fresh, not dried or moldy.

funFact: Eggplants are technically berries and members of the nightshade family, along with tomatoes, potatoes, and tobacco.
storageTip: Store at room temperature and use within 2 days, or refrigerate in the crisper drawer for up to 5 days. Cold temperatures can damage the texture if stored too long.

name: Green Beans

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be bright green with a smooth surface. Avoid beans with visible bulges from oversized seeds inside.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should snap cleanly when bent in half. If they bend without breaking, they are old and rubbery.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Slender, young beans are more tender and flavorful than thick, mature ones with prominent seeds.

funFact: Green beans were one of the first New World foods to be adopted in Europe after Spanish explorers brought them back in the 16th century.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a plastic bag in the crisper drawer for up to 7 days. To freeze, blanch for 3 minutes first, then ice-bath and dry before bagging.

name: Kale

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should be deeply colored (dark green to blue-green) and crisp with no yellowing or brown spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should feel sturdy and firm, not limp or slimy. Smaller leaves are more tender for salads.

ripenessTips.title: Check stems
ripenessTips.description: Stems should be moist at the cut end and firm. Dried-out or slimy stems mean old kale.

funFact: Kale becomes sweeter after exposure to frost, similar to Brussels sprouts, as the plant converts starch to sugar to protect its cells.
storageTip: Wrap in a damp paper towel and store in a loose bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. Do not wash before storing as moisture accelerates decay.

name: Peas

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Pods should be bright green, plump, and slightly shiny. Dull, yellowish, or dry pods are past their prime.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: For shelling peas, the pods should feel full and firm. For sugar snaps and snow peas, they should be crisp and flat.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Snap a pod in half: it should make a clean, audible snap. A limp bend means they are old.

funFact: Gregor Mendel used peas to discover the fundamental laws of genetics in the 1860s, making the humble pea foundational to modern biology.
storageTip: Eat as quickly as possible; like corn, peas begin converting sugar to starch immediately after picking. Refrigerate in a bag for up to 3 days. Freeze quickly if not eating right away.

name: Pumpkin

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be a deep, uniform orange (or color typical for variety) with no soft spots, cuts, or mold.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: The rind should be very hard and resist a thumbnail pressed into it. Soft rind means it is not fully mature.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Knock on it. A ripe pumpkin sounds hollow, similar to a drum.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: A dry, corky stem indicates maturity. Never carry a pumpkin by its stem, as it can break off and invite rot.

funFact: Pumpkins are about 90 percent water and are technically a fruit because they develop from the flowering part of the plant and contain seeds.
storageTip: Cure in a warm spot for 10 days, then store in a cool, dry place for up to 3 months. Cut pumpkin can be refrigerated for a week or frozen for months.

name: Radish

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be brightly colored with smooth, unblemished skin. Avoid cracked or oversized radishes, which may be pithy inside.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be rock-hard and firm. A spongy or soft radish has a woody, hollow center.

ripenessTips.title: Check greens
ripenessTips.description: If greens are attached, they should look fresh and perky, not slimy or yellow.

funFact: Radishes were among the first European crops planted in the Americas and were even grown by astronauts on the International Space Station.
storageTip: Remove greens right away and store radishes in a bag in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks. To restore crispness, soak in ice water for 30 minutes.

name: Spinach

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should be vibrant dark green and crisp. Yellow, wilted, or slimy leaves indicate age.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should feel springy and resilient, not limp or soggy. Thicker leaves hold up better in cooking.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Should have a fresh, earthy scent. A sour or off smell means it has started to decay.

funFact: Spinach loses about 90 percent of its volume when cooked because the heat breaks down the cell walls and releases all the water stored inside.
storageTip: Store in a bag lined with paper towels in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Do not wash before storing. Excess moisture is the top cause of quick spoilage.

name: Sweet Potato

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Skin should be smooth and uniform in color with no cracks, soft spots, or sprouts.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be very firm throughout. Any soft or mushy areas indicate rot that will spread.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Choose medium-sized sweet potatoes for the best texture. Very large ones can be fibrous and less sweet.

funFact: Despite the name, sweet potatoes are not related to regular potatoes at all; they belong to the morning glory family.
storageTip: Store in a cool, dark, well-ventilated place (not the refrigerator) for up to a month. Cold temperatures convert starches to sugars and alter the texture.

name: Tomato

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sniff near the stem. A ripe tomato has a rich, earthy, sweet tomato smell. No smell usually means no flavor.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should give slightly to gentle pressure but bounce back. Hard means underripe; very soft means overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Color should be deep and uniform for the variety. The bottom (blossom end) should be the same color as the sides.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A ripe tomato is heavy for its size, indicating juiciness and dense flesh.

funFact: Tomatoes were once considered poisonous in Europe because wealthy people who ate them from pewter plates got sick from the lead leaching into the acidic juice.
storageTip: Never refrigerate unripe tomatoes; cold kills the flavor enzymes permanently. Store stem-side down at room temperature. Once fully ripe, eat within a day or two.

name: Zucchini

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be dark green and glossy with no nicks, soft spots, or shriveled ends.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm from end to end. Soft spots or sponginess indicate it is old or was damaged.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Smaller zucchini (6 to 8 inches) have the best flavor and texture. Large ones are watery and seedy.

funFact: A single zucchini plant can produce 6 to 10 pounds of fruit in a season, which is why gardeners are famously known for giving away their surplus.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a perforated bag in the crisper drawer for up to a week. Do not cut until ready to use, as exposed flesh deteriorates quickly.

name: Lettuce

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should be crisp, vibrant, and free from brown edges, slime, or wilting. Avoid heads with a pinkish tint on the ribs.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel springy and light for its size. A head that feels too dense or heavy may be over-mature and bitter.

ripenessTips.title: Check base
ripenessTips.description: The cut end at the base should look fresh and white, not brown or dried out.

funFact: Ancient Egyptians first cultivated lettuce not for eating but for the oil from its seeds; it was later adopted as a food crop by the Greeks and Romans.
storageTip: Wrap in a damp paper towel and store in a loose bag in the crisper drawer for up to a week. Keep away from apples and bananas which cause browning.

name: Leek

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The white and light green portion should be clean, firm, and long. Dark green tops should be vibrant, not yellowed.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm and crisp from root to top. Avoid leeks that feel soft, slimy, or rubbery.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Medium-sized leeks (about 1 to 1.5 inches in diameter) are more tender than very thick ones, which can be tough.

funFact: The leek is the national emblem of Wales; legend says Welsh soldiers wore leeks on their helmets to distinguish themselves in battle.
storageTip: Store untrimmed and unwashed in a loose plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks. Do not trim until ready to cook, and rinse thoroughly between layers to remove trapped dirt.

name: Blackberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Berries should be uniformly deep black, not red or purple.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Plump and firm but not hard. Avoid mushy berries.

ripenessTips.title: Check
ripenessTips.description: Should release easily from the stem when gently pulled.

funFact: A single blackberry is actually a cluster of tiny fruits called drupelets, each containing its own seed.
storageTip: Refrigerate unwashed in a single layer for 2-3 days. Wash just before eating.

name: Raspberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be bright, evenly colored, and free of mold.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Plump and dry to the touch. Wet berries spoil quickly.

funFact: Raspberries are a member of the rose family and there are over 200 species worldwide.
storageTip: Store in a single layer in the fridge for 1-2 days. Do not wash until ready to eat.

name: Boysenberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Deep maroon-purple color when fully ripe.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Soft and slightly yielding, but not mushy.

funFact: The boysenberry was created in the 1920s by Rudolph Boysen by crossing raspberries, blackberries, and loganberries.
storageTip: Very perishable. Refrigerate and consume within 1-2 days.

name: Clementine

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright orange color with a glossy, smooth skin.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy for its size, indicating juiciness.

funFact: Clementines are seedless because they are the result of a natural mutation, not genetic modification.
storageTip: Keep at room temperature for a week or refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

name: Tangerine

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Rich orange color. Some green is okay near the stem.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Heavy for its size with slightly loose, pebbly skin.

funFact: Tangerines got their name from Tangier, Morocco, the port from which they were first shipped to Europe.
storageTip: Store at room temperature for a few days or refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

name: Blood Orange

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: May have a reddish blush on the rind but not always. Inside is the true test.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and heavy for its size.

funFact: The deep red color comes from anthocyanins, the same pigments found in blueberries and red cabbage.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to 2 weeks. Best eaten fresh to enjoy the color.

name: Lime

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright green skin. Yellowing means overripe but sweeter.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm but gives slightly when squeezed. Should feel heavy.

funFact: British sailors earned the nickname 'limeys' because they ate limes to prevent scurvy on long voyages.
storageTip: Room temperature for a week, refrigerate for up to 3 weeks. Juice can be frozen in ice cube trays.

name: Key Lime

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Yellowish-green when ripe, not bright green.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel slightly soft and heavy for its small size.

funFact: Key limes are named after the Florida Keys, where they were once the dominant citrus crop.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to 2 weeks. They dry out quickly at room temperature.

name: Meyer Lemon

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Deep yellow-orange when ripe, smoother than regular lemons.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Wonderfully fragrant with a floral, herbal scent.

funFact: Meyer lemons are actually a cross between a lemon and a mandarin orange, discovered by Frank Meyer in China in 1908.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to 2 weeks. More delicate than regular lemons.

name: Kumquat

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright orange and plump. Avoid dull or shriveled fruit.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm with a bit of give. The skin is the sweet part!

funFact: Kumquats are the only citrus fruit where you eat the peel — it's sweet while the juice is sour.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a sealed bag for up to 2 weeks.

name: Coconut

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Shake it — you should hear sloshing water inside.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Choose coconuts with dry, brown eyes (the three dark spots).

funFact: The name 'coconut' comes from 16th-century Portuguese sailors who thought the three holes looked like a face (coco means grinning face).
storageTip: Whole coconuts last 2-3 months at room temperature. Once opened, refrigerate flesh for up to a week.

name: Dragon Fruit

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright, even color with just a few brown spots. Avoid very brown skin.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should give slightly like a ripe avocado when pressed.

funFact: Dragon fruit comes from a cactus and the flowers only bloom for one night, earning the name 'moonflower'.
storageTip: Store ripe fruit in the fridge for up to 5 days. Cut fruit should be eaten within 1-2 days.

name: Passion Fruit

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Wrinkly skin is actually a good sign — it means the fruit is ripe and sweet.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy for its size, indicating lots of juice and pulp.

funFact: The passion in 'passion fruit' refers to the Passion of Christ — Spanish missionaries saw symbolism in the flower's structure.
storageTip: Ripe fruit at room temperature for 2-3 days. Refrigerate for up to a week. Pulp freezes well.

name: Guava

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Ripe guava has a strong, sweet, musky fragrance.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Gives slightly when gently pressed, like a ripe pear.

funFact: A single guava has 4 times more vitamin C than an orange.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature, then refrigerate for up to 4 days.

name: Papaya

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Skin turns from green to yellow-orange as it ripens.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Gives to gentle pressure like a ripe avocado.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sweet, fragrant aroma at the base when ripe.

funFact: Papaya contains papain, an enzyme so powerful it was once used to tenderize meat commercially.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature. Once ripe, refrigerate for up to 3 days.

name: Lychee

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright red-pink shell with no brown patches.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Shell should feel bumpy and slightly firm, not dried out.

funFact: Lychee has been cultivated in China for over 2,000 years and was a favorite of the imperial court.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a plastic bag for up to 2 weeks. The shell may brown but the flesh stays fresh.

name: Plum

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Rich, deep color with a powdery bloom (white coating) which is natural.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Gives slightly at the tip when gently pressed.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sweet, fruity aroma when ripe.

funFact: Dried plums are called prunes, and it takes about 3 pounds of fresh plums to make 1 pound of prunes.
storageTip: Ripen on the counter, then refrigerate for up to 5 days.

name: Nectarine

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Strong sweet fragrance at the stem end.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Gives slightly to gentle pressure. Too soft means overripe.

funFact: Nectarines are genetically almost identical to peaches — the smooth skin is caused by a single recessive gene.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature, then refrigerate for up to 5 days.

name: Honeydew

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Creamy yellow skin, not green or white.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Slightly waxy and heavy. The blossom end should give a little.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sweet, musky fragrance at the blossom end.

funFact: Honeydew melons are about 90% water, making them one of the most hydrating fruits available.
storageTip: Whole uncut melons last a week at room temperature. Cut melon keeps 3-4 days refrigerated.

name: Date

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Plump with glossy, slightly wrinkled skin. Avoid very dry or crystallized dates.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be soft and slightly sticky, not hard or dried out.

funFact: Date palms can produce fruit for over 100 years, and a single tree can yield up to 200 pounds of dates annually.
storageTip: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for a month, or refrigerate for up to 6 months.

name: Starfruit

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright yellow with slightly browned ridges. Green means unripe.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Fragrant, sweet aroma when ripe.

funFact: When sliced crosswise, starfruit creates perfect five-pointed star shapes, which is how it got its name.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature, then refrigerate for up to a week.

name: Jackfruit

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Strong sweet fragrance. If it smells fermented, it is overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Yields slightly to pressure. Spines should be soft, not sharp.

funFact: Jackfruit is the largest tree-borne fruit in the world, reaching up to 80 pounds. Young jackfruit has a pulled-pork-like texture when cooked.
storageTip: Whole fruit keeps at room temp for a few days. Cut pieces refrigerate for up to 5 days.

name: Longan

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Light tan-brown shell, evenly colored without cracks.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Shell should crack easily revealing translucent white flesh.

funFact: Longan means 'dragon eye' in Chinese — the translucent flesh with a dark seed in the center resembles an eyeball.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a perforated bag for up to 2 weeks.

name: Rambutan

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright red with green-tipped soft spines. Brown spines mean old.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Slightly firm. Shell should peel away easily.

funFact: Rambutan means 'hairy' in Malay, referring to the soft spines covering the fruit.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to a week. Best eaten within a few days of purchase.

name: Quince

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Golden yellow when ripe. Some fuzz on the skin is normal.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Intensely fragrant with a floral, apple-like aroma.

funFact: Quince is too hard and astringent to eat raw, but cooking transforms it into a beautiful pink-red with a honey-like flavor.
storageTip: Keeps for 2-3 months in the refrigerator. One of the longest-storing fruits.

name: Tamarind

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Brown brittle shell that cracks easily. Avoid pods with holes.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Pod should feel full and heavy, not hollow or light.

funFact: Tamarind is used in Worcestershire sauce, giving it the distinctive tangy flavor.
storageTip: Whole pods keep for months at room temperature. Paste stores for a year in the fridge.

name: Cherimoya

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Gives to gentle pressure like a ripe avocado. Should feel heavy.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Skin may turn slightly brown when ripe; some browning is ok.

funFact: Mark Twain called cherimoya 'the most delicious fruit known to men.' Its flavor is often described as a blend of banana, pineapple, and strawberry.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature. Once soft, eat immediately or refrigerate for 1-2 days.

name: Soursop

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should yield to gentle pressure when ripe. Skin turns slightly yellow-green.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sweet, pineapple-like fragrance when ripe.

funFact: Soursop is called guanabana in Latin America and is one of the most popular tropical juice flavors.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature. Once ripe, pulp can be frozen for months.

name: Mamey Sapote

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Scratch the skin — if pink-orange shows underneath, it is ripe.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Brown rough skin. Flesh inside should be salmon-orange.

funFact: Mamey sapote is the key ingredient in Cuban batidos (milkshakes) and Mexican ice cream.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature until it yields to pressure. Refrigerate when ripe for 3-4 days.

name: Tuna (Prickly Pear)

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Deep color (red, purple, or yellow depending on variety). Avoid green fruit.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Gives slightly when pressed. Handle carefully — tiny glochid spines!

funFact: Mexico produces 90% of the world's prickly pear fruit and the nopal cactus even appears on the Mexican flag.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to a week. Use tongs or thick gloves to handle, then peel.

name: Tejocote

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Orange-yellow color, similar to a small crabapple.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm when fresh. Used cooked in ponche (fruit punch).

funFact: Tejocote is essential to Mexican ponche, the traditional warm fruit punch served during Christmas posadas.
storageTip: Store in a cool, dry place for up to 2 weeks. Often sold in syrup or preserved.

name: Mulberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Deep purple-black when fully ripe. Red ones are still unripe.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Soft and plump. Falls from the tree when ripe.

funFact: Mulberry leaves are the sole food source for silkworms, making the tree essential to the silk industry for thousands of years.
storageTip: Extremely perishable — eat same day or refrigerate for 1-2 days max.

name: Rhubarb

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Firm, crisp stalks with good color. Avoid limp or wilted stalks.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should snap cleanly when bent, like celery.

funFact: Rhubarb is technically a vegetable but is legally classified as a fruit in the US (since 1947) because of how it is used in cooking.
storageTip: Wrap in foil and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks. Freezes well for baking.

name: Plantain

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Green = starchy (frying), yellow = semi-sweet, black = sweet (maduros).

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firmness depends on desired use. Firm for tostones, soft for maduros.

funFact: Plantains are a staple food for over 100 million people in Africa and Latin America, eaten cooked rather than raw.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature. Green plantains take 1-2 weeks to fully ripen to black.

name: Yuzu

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Yellow and slightly bumpy skin when ripe. Green yuzu is used for its zest.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Intensely aromatic — floral citrus scent.

funFact: In Japan, floating yuzu in hot baths during the winter solstice (yuzu-yu) is believed to ward off colds.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to 2 weeks. The zest and juice both freeze excellently.

name: Gooseberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Color depends on variety: green, red, or golden when ripe.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Slightly soft. Tart varieties are firm, dessert types are softer.

funFact: Gooseberries were once so popular in England that competitive gooseberry-growing shows have been held since the 1700s.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to 3 weeks. They freeze beautifully for pies and jams.

name: Red Currant

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright, translucent red berries in clusters. Avoid dull or wrinkled berries.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and plump on the stem.

funFact: Red currants contain more vitamin C per gram than oranges. They were banned in the US for decades because they can spread a fungus harmful to pine trees.
storageTip: Refrigerate on the stem for up to a week. Freeze for longer storage.

name: Durian

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Strong aroma is normal! Sour or alcoholic smell means overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Shake it — seeds should rattle slightly inside a ripe durian.

funFact: Durian is banned from many hotels and public transport in Southeast Asia due to its pungent smell, yet it is called the 'king of fruits.'
storageTip: Eat fresh. Wrapped flesh can be refrigerated 2-3 days. Freezing makes it ice-cream-like.

name: Nopales

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Small to medium pads, bright green, firm. Avoid large, thick, fibrous ones.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and moist when cut. Should not be limp or dry.

funFact: Nopales have been a staple of Mexican cuisine for over 12,000 years and are depicted on the Mexican coat of arms.
storageTip: Wrap in damp paper towels and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

name: Chayote

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Light green, firm, without wrinkles or soft spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and heavy for its size.

funFact: Every part of the chayote plant is edible — fruit, seed, leaves, and even the tuberous root.
storageTip: Refrigerate unwrapped for up to 3 weeks. One of the longest-lasting fresh vegetables.

name: Jicama

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Smooth, unblemished tan skin. Medium size is sweetest.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Very firm and heavy. Should not have any soft spots.

funFact: Jicama is a legume that grows underground. Only the root is edible — the rest of the plant is toxic.
storageTip: Store whole in a cool, dry place for 2-3 weeks. Cut jicama refrigerates for about a week.

name: Tomatillo

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Fills or bursts its papery husk. Bright green for tangy, yellowish for sweeter.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and sticky under the husk — stickiness is natural and desired.

funFact: Despite the name, tomatillos are not baby tomatoes. They are more closely related to gooseberries.
storageTip: Keep in husks and refrigerate for up to 3 weeks. Remove husks and wash before using.

name: Jalapeno

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Firm, smooth, deep green. White lines (corking) indicate more heat.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and crisp. Red jalapenos are ripe and slightly sweeter.

funFact: Jalapenos are named after Xalapa, the capital of Veracruz, Mexico. When smoked and dried, they become chipotle peppers.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a paper bag for up to 2 weeks.

name: Serrano

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Glossy, firm, and bright green. Red serranos are fully mature.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and smooth, no wrinkles.

funFact: Serrano means 'from the mountains' in Spanish — they originate from the mountainous regions of Puebla and Hidalgo.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to 2 weeks. Can be frozen whole for later use.

name: Habanero

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright orange, red, or yellow depending on variety. Shiny and plump.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm with smooth skin. Wrinkled skin means it is past peak.

funFact: Habaneros are 100 times hotter than jalapenos. The Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico is considered their place of origin.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to 2 weeks. They freeze very well and maintain their heat.

name: Poblano

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Dark green, almost black. Large and heart-shaped.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and heavy with glossy skin.

funFact: When dried, poblano peppers become ancho chiles — the most widely used dried chile in Mexican cuisine.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a paper bag for up to a week. Roast and freeze for longer storage.

name: Calabaza

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Hard rind with even color. No soft spots or cracks.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Very hard shell and heavy for its size.

funFact: Calabaza is the generic Spanish word for squash and has been cultivated in the Americas for over 7,000 years.
storageTip: Whole squash keeps for months in a cool, dry place. Cut pieces refrigerate for a week.

name: Epazote

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Fresh, bright green leaves with no yellowing or wilting.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Strong, pungent, slightly medicinal aroma — this is normal.

funFact: Epazote has been used in Mexican cooking for centuries both as a seasoning and as a traditional remedy to reduce the gassiness of beans.
storageTip: Wrap in damp paper towel and refrigerate for up to a week. Dries well.

name: Cilantro

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright green, perky leaves. Avoid yellowing or slimy stems.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Fresh, bright herbal scent. Wilted cilantro loses its aroma.

funFact: Whether you love or hate cilantro may be genetic — a variation in the OR6A2 gene makes it taste like soap to some people.
storageTip: Place stems in a jar of water, cover loosely with a bag, and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

name: Parsley

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright green, crisp stems. Flat-leaf has more flavor than curly.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Fresh, clean herbal aroma.

funFact: Parsley was used by ancient Romans to mask bad breath and as a deodorizer at banquets.
storageTip: Store like cilantro — stems in water, covered, in the fridge. Lasts up to 3 weeks.

name: Basil

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Vibrant green with no dark spots or wilting.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Intensely aromatic when you rub a leaf.

funFact: There are over 60 varieties of basil. In Italy, placing basil on a windowsill was once a signal of romantic interest.
storageTip: Do NOT refrigerate — it turns black. Keep stems in water at room temperature like flowers.

name: Mint

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright green, perky leaves without dark spots.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Strong, cool menthol aroma.

funFact: Mint is so vigorous it is considered invasive in many areas — gardeners recommend growing it in containers.
storageTip: Wrap in damp paper towel and refrigerate for up to a week. Freezes well in ice cube trays with water.

name: Dill

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Feathery fronds should be bright green and fragrant.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Fresh, anise-like aroma.

funFact: The word dill comes from the Norse word 'dilla' meaning to lull or soothe — it was used as a calming remedy.
storageTip: Wrap in damp paper towel and refrigerate for 1-2 weeks. Loses flavor when dried.

name: Rosemary

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Deep green needle-like leaves, no browning.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Strong, piney, aromatic scent.

funFact: Rosemary has been associated with memory improvement since ancient Greece — students wore it in their hair during exams.
storageTip: Wrap in damp paper towel and refrigerate for up to 3 weeks. One of the hardiest herbs.

name: Thyme

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Tiny green-grey leaves on woody stems. No browning or drying.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Warm, earthy, slightly minty aroma.

funFact: Ancient Egyptians used thyme in the embalming process, and Roman soldiers bathed in thyme water for vigor before battle.
storageTip: Refrigerate wrapped in damp paper towel for up to 2 weeks. Dries very well.

name: Oregano

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Small oval leaves, bright to dark green.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Strong, warm, slightly bitter aroma.

funFact: Mexican oregano and Mediterranean oregano are actually different plant species with distinct flavor profiles.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to a week. Dried oregano is actually more concentrated in flavor than fresh.

name: Sage

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Silvery-green velvety leaves without brown edges.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Warm, piney, slightly peppery aroma.

funFact: The word sage comes from the Latin 'salvere' meaning 'to be saved' — it was considered a cure-all in medieval medicine.
storageTip: Wrap in damp paper towel and refrigerate for up to a week.

name: Swiss Chard

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Glossy leaves with brightly colored stems (red, yellow, or white).

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Crisp stems and tender leaves, not wilted.

funFact: Despite its name, Swiss chard is actually native to the Mediterranean — a Swiss botanist cataloged it in the 19th century.
storageTip: Wrap in damp paper towel and refrigerate for up to a week.

name: Collard Greens

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Dark green, smooth leaves without yellowing or holes.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and crisp, not limp.

funFact: Collard greens actually improve in flavor after a light frost, which converts starches to sugars.
storageTip: Wrap in damp paper towel and refrigerate for up to 5 days.

name: Mustard Greens

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright green with no yellowing. Smaller leaves are more tender.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Crisp and fresh, not slimy.

funFact: Mustard greens are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown in the Himalayan region over 5,000 years ago.
storageTip: Refrigerate wrapped in damp paper towel for 3-5 days.

name: Arugula

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright green oak-shaped leaves. Smaller = milder, larger = more peppery.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Peppery, slightly nutty aroma.

funFact: Arugula was considered an aphrodisiac in ancient Rome and was often grown near the statue of Priapus.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a loose bag for 2-3 days. Very perishable.

name: Watercress

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright green leaves with crisp stems. Avoid yellowing or wilting.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Crisp and fresh with a peppery bite.

funFact: Watercress was a staple of Roman soldiers' diets and grows naturally in shallow streams.
storageTip: Store stems in water like a bouquet. Use within 2-3 days.

name: Endive

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Pale yellow-white with compact, torpedo-shaped heads.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and crisp leaves tightly packed.

funFact: Belgian endive is grown in complete darkness to keep it pale and mild in flavor.
storageTip: Wrap in paper towel and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks. Keep away from light.

name: Radicchio

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Deep burgundy leaves with white ribs. Compact and heavy head.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and dense, not spongy.

funFact: Radicchio belongs to the chicory family and the bitterness mellows significantly when grilled.
storageTip: Refrigerate wrapped in paper towel for up to 2 weeks.

name: Bok Choy

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Crisp white stalks with vibrant dark green leaves.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm stalks that snap when bent.

funFact: Bok choy has been cultivated in China for over 5,000 years and is a member of the cabbage family.
storageTip: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose bag for up to a week.

name: Napa Cabbage

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Tall, oblong head with pale green-white crinkled leaves.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Compact and heavy. Leaves should be crisp.

funFact: Napa cabbage is the key ingredient in kimchi and is different from regular cabbage in both taste and texture.
storageTip: Refrigerate whole for up to 2 weeks. Cut portions last about a week.

name: Turnip

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Smooth, unblemished skin. Small to medium size is sweetest.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and heavy for its size.

funFact: Before pumpkins were available in Ireland, turnips were carved into jack-o-lanterns for Halloween.
storageTip: Remove greens and refrigerate roots for 2-3 weeks. Cook the greens separately.

name: Rutabaga

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Purple-tinged top with yellow bottom. Smooth and firm.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Very heavy for its size and rock-hard when fresh.

funFact: Rutabagas are a cross between turnips and cabbage, first bred in Scandinavia in the 17th century.
storageTip: Store in a cool root cellar for months, or refrigerate for up to 3 weeks.

name: Parsnip

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Cream-colored, smooth skin. Medium size is best.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm, like a carrot. Avoid limp or rubbery ones.

funFact: Parsnips become sweeter after frost because the cold converts their starches into sugar.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a perforated bag for 2-3 weeks.

name: Daikon Radish

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: White, smooth, straight. Avoid cracked or spotted ones.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and heavy. Should not bend.

funFact: Japan alone produces over 1 million tons of daikon annually — it is the most consumed vegetable in the country.
storageTip: Refrigerate wrapped in plastic for up to 2 weeks.

name: Kohlrabi

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Small to medium bulbs (tennis ball size). Can be green or purple.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and smooth. Large ones can be woody.

funFact: Kohlrabi means 'cabbage turnip' in German. Despite its alien appearance, it tastes like a mild, sweet broccoli stem.
storageTip: Refrigerate for 2-3 weeks. Remove leaves and store separately.

name: Cassava

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bark-like skin should be intact. Flesh should be pure white.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Very firm. Avoid soft spots or blue-grey streaks in the flesh.

funFact: Cassava feeds over half a billion people worldwide and is the third-largest source of carbohydrates in the tropics.
storageTip: Use within a few days of purchase. Peel and freeze for longer storage. Must be cooked — never eat raw.

name: Taro

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Brown hairy skin. Firm with no soft spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Hard and heavy. Should not give when pressed.

funFact: Taro is one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown in Southeast Asia for over 10,000 years. It is the base for Hawaiian poi.
storageTip: Store in a cool, dark, dry place for 1-2 weeks. Must be cooked before eating.

name: Butternut Squash

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Uniform beige skin with no green patches. Matte finish, not shiny.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Very hard shell and heavy. No soft spots.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Knock on it — should sound hollow.

funFact: A single butternut squash vine can produce 10-20 squash per season and one squash can weigh up to 5 pounds.
storageTip: Keeps 2-3 months in a cool, dark place. Cut squash refrigerates for about a week.

name: Acorn Squash

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Dark green with an orange patch on the bottom where it rested.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Hard rind and heavy. The stem should be dry.

funFact: Acorn squash gets its name from its acorn-like shape and is one of the oldest domesticated squashes.
storageTip: Keeps 1-2 months in a cool, dry spot.

name: Spaghetti Squash

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright yellow all over. No green spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Hard rind, heavy for its size.

funFact: When cooked, the flesh separates into spaghetti-like strands — a natural, low-carb pasta alternative.
storageTip: Keeps 1-2 months in a cool, dry place.

name: Delicata Squash

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Cream-colored with green stripes. No soft spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm. Lighter than other winter squash.

funFact: Delicata is one of the few winter squashes with an edible skin, making it the easiest to prepare.
storageTip: Shorter shelf life than other winter squash — use within 3-4 weeks.

name: Summer Squash

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Small to medium size with glossy skin. Large ones are seedy.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm but tender skin you can dent with a fingernail.

funFact: Summer squash are harvested immature, while winter squash are left to fully mature on the vine.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to a week. Do not store in plastic — they need air circulation.

name: Scallion

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright white bulbs with crisp, dark green tops.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and crisp, not slimy or wilted.

funFact: Scallions, green onions, and spring onions are often used interchangeably though they are slightly different varieties.
storageTip: Stand upright in a glass of water in the fridge for up to 2 weeks.

name: Shallot

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Dry, papery copper-colored skin. Firm with no sprouting.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and heavy with no soft spots.

funFact: Shallots are prized in French cuisine for their delicate, sweeter flavor compared to regular onions.
storageTip: Store in a cool, dark, dry place for up to a month.

name: Garlic

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm, plump bulbs with tight cloves. Avoid soft or spongy.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Dry, papery skin intact. No green shoots.

funFact: China produces 80% of the world's garlic — over 20 million tons per year.
storageTip: Store in a cool, dry, dark place with airflow for 3-6 months. Do not refrigerate whole bulbs.

name: Ginger

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Smooth, taut skin. Wrinkled skin means old and fibrous.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and heavy. Should snap cleanly when broken.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Spicy, warm aroma when skin is scratched.

funFact: Ginger has been used medicinally for over 5,000 years and contains gingerol, which has powerful anti-inflammatory properties.
storageTip: Store unpeeled in the fridge for up to 3 weeks, or freeze for months.

name: Turmeric

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Deep orange flesh when cut. Firm, small fingers.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and heavy. Skin should be tight, not wrinkled.

funFact: Turmeric gives curry its yellow color and has been used as a fabric dye for thousands of years in South Asia.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a sealed bag for 2-3 weeks. Freezes well for months. Warning: it stains everything!

name: Snow Peas

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Flat, bright green pods. You should be able to see the peas faintly through the pod.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Crisp and snap easily. Should not be limp.

funFact: Snow peas are called 'mange tout' (eat everything) in French because the entire pod is eaten.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a perforated bag for 3-5 days. Do not wash until ready to use.

name: Sugar Snap Peas

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Plump, rounded pods with bright green color.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Crisp and snappy. Should pop when bent.

funFact: Sugar snap peas were only invented in 1979 by crossing snow peas with garden peas. They are a relatively modern vegetable.
storageTip: Refrigerate for 3-5 days. Best eaten as fresh as possible.

name: Edamame

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright green, plump pods with 2-3 beans visible inside.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm pods that pop open easily when squeezed.

funFact: Edamame means 'stem beans' in Japanese and they have been eaten in East Asia for over 2,000 years.
storageTip: Fresh pods refrigerate for 2-3 days. Blanch and freeze for months.

name: Lima Bean

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Plump green pods for fresh limas. Dry pods for dried beans.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Pods should be full and firm with visible bean outlines.

funFact: Lima beans are named after Lima, Peru, where they have been cultivated since 6000 BC.
storageTip: Shell and refrigerate fresh beans for 2-3 days. Freeze blanched beans for months.

name: Okra

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright green, 2-4 inches long. Larger pods are tough and woody.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm but tender. Should snap, not bend.

funFact: Okra was brought to the Americas from Africa during the slave trade and is now a cornerstone of Southern US cuisine (gumbo).
storageTip: Refrigerate dry in a paper bag for 2-3 days. Very perishable.

name: Fennel

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: White to pale green bulb with fresh green fronds.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and compact bulb. Avoid soft or spreading layers.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Mild anise/licorice aroma.

funFact: Every part of the fennel plant is edible — the bulb, stalks, fronds, pollen, and seeds each have culinary uses.
storageTip: Refrigerate for up to 2 weeks. Remove fronds and store separately.

name: Celery

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright green stalks that are crisp and tightly bunched.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and snappy. Should not bend without breaking.

funFact: Celery is so low in calories that it was long believed to be a 'negative calorie food' — though this is technically a myth.
storageTip: Wrap in aluminum foil and refrigerate for up to 4 weeks. Foil keeps it crispier than plastic.

name: Shiitake Mushroom

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Firm, dry caps with white gills. Avoid slimy or dark spots.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Earthy, woodsy aroma. Off smells mean they are past prime.

funFact: Shiitake means 'shii tree mushroom' in Japanese and have been cultivated for over 1,000 years on oak logs.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a paper bag for up to 10 days. Never store in plastic.

name: Oyster Mushroom

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Fan-shaped, light grey to cream colored. Edges should be smooth.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Mild, pleasant anise-like scent. No sour smell.

funFact: Oyster mushrooms are one of the few carnivorous mushrooms — they produce toxins that paralyze tiny roundworms for nitrogen.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a paper bag for 5-7 days. Very delicate — handle gently.

name: Bitter Melon

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright green and firm for less bitterness. Yellow means very ripe and more bitter.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm with bumpy texture. Should not be soft.

funFact: Bitter melon is one of the most bitter foods on earth and is used in traditional medicine across Asia to help manage blood sugar.
storageTip: Refrigerate for 4-5 days. Soaking sliced pieces in salt water reduces bitterness.

name: Bamboo Shoots

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Ivory white with tight, compact layers. No brown or slimy spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm and heavy. Should not feel hollow.

funFact: Bamboo is the fastest-growing plant on earth — some species grow over 3 feet in a single day. Fresh shoots are a spring delicacy.
storageTip: Refrigerate fresh unpeeled shoots for up to 2 weeks. Must be boiled before eating to remove toxins.

name: Water Chestnut

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Dark brown skin, round and plump. No wrinkles.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Very firm with crisp, white flesh inside.

funFact: Water chestnuts are not nuts — they are aquatic tubers that grow in marshes and stay crunchy even after cooking.
storageTip: Refrigerate unpeeled for up to 2 weeks. Peeled water chestnuts last 2-3 days submerged in water.

name: Bean Sprouts

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright white with firm, plump sprouts. No browning.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Should smell fresh and clean, not sour.

funFact: Bean sprouts can be grown at home in just 3-5 days, making them one of the easiest vegetables to grow year-round.
storageTip: Refrigerate submerged in water for 2-3 days, changing water daily. Very perishable.

name: Chinese Broccoli

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Thick stems with dark green leaves and small white flowers.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Firm, crisp stems that snap. Not limp or woody.

funFact: Chinese broccoli (gai lan) is more closely related to regular broccoli than bok choy, despite its leafy appearance.
storageTip: Refrigerate in a damp paper towel for 3-5 days.

name: Hoja Santa

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Large, heart-shaped, velvety dark green leaves.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Complex anise-sassafras-mint aroma.

funFact: Hoja santa means 'sacred leaf' in Spanish. It is used to wrap tamales and fish in Oaxacan cuisine.
storageTip: Wrap in damp paper towel and refrigerate for up to a week.

name: Horseradish

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Firm, tan root with no mold or soft spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Very hard and solid. Should not be spongy.

funFact: The heat of horseradish is caused by allyl isothiocyanate, which is released when the root cells are crushed. Unlike chile heat, it hits the nose more than the tongue.
storageTip: Refrigerate whole root for 1-2 months. Once grated, use quickly — flavor fades fast.

name: Malanga

ripenessTips.title: Look
